item.title: Why Video Compresses 100×: Redundancy, YUV, I/P/B Frames and GOP
item.description:
The later posts on browser codec selection and the streaming protocol panorama keep leaning on H.264, I-frames and GOP — this post fills in the foundation first: what actually happens when a stream of pixels turns into a few Mbps. No math derivations — mechanisms, each tied to its engineering consequence (latency, seeking, corruption, storage).

Start with some arithmetic.

How big is uncompressed video

One 1080p (1920×1080), 30fps, 8bit RGB stream:

text
1
2
3
4

pixels per frame = 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600
bytes per frame = 2,073,600 × 3 (RGB) ≈ 5.93 MB
per second = 5.93 MB × 30 ≈ 178 MB/s
bitrate ≈ 1.49 Gbps

That is 10.7 GB per minute. 4K (3840×2160) multiplies by another 4: ~42.7 GB/min. Sixteen surveillance cameras recording for a month at these rates is beyond any storage system. In practice 1080p surveillance streams run 2–8 Mbps — a compression ratio on the order of several hundred to one. Compression is not an optimization; it is the precondition for video existing at all.

item.title: H.264 / H.265 / H.266 Web Frontend Playback: Which Generation to Pick in 2026
item.description: The previous post traced bitstream structures from H.265 through AV1/AVS; this one comes back to the browser: which generation should you actually use. In the MiBee NVR surveillance-dashboard project, should the frontend pull H.264 or H.265 from all 16 cameras? A seemingly simple question that gets deeper the more you dig. H.265 needs only half the bitrate of H.264 at the same quality, saving both bandwidth and storage. But plenty of online sources still claim “H.265 browser support is poor, Firefox doesn’t support it, you need to install extensions.” Which of these claims still hold?

item.title: Streaming Protocols Deep Dive: 14 Technologies, Their Limits, and Selection Guide
item.description:
The four codec posts covered how video gets compressed; this one covers how it gets delivered. These 14 streaming technologies don’t operate in the same layer. A complete live streaming pipeline typically follows:

Camera/Encoder → Ingest (RTMP / SRT / RIST / WebRTC-WHIP / WebTransport) → Transcode → Delivery (HLS / LL-HLS / DASH / LL-DASH / HESP / HTTP-FLV) → Viewers

Start by identifying which segment of the pipeline you’re working on, not by asking “which is better.”

item.title: PTZ Latency End-to-End: From Encoding to Transport Optimization
item.description:
The operator calls: the PTZ feed is several seconds behind. Push the joystick and the far end reacts long after. Ops swaps the camera first—no change; suspects the network—RTT measured, normal; finally shrinks the player buffer—the problem disappears on the spot.

That is not a skit; it is the standard path of a “latency complaint”: swap hardware first, check the network second, and only then get to the real problem. The previous post in this series, “The Two Devils of PTZ Cameras,” named latency one of the two devils. This one tears it apart: where each millisecond goes, what can be optimized, and what is a hard protocol limitation.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.13.0 Performance Self-Benchmark: Capacity and Resource Curves on Three Hardware Tiers
item.description:
Choosing an NVR keeps running into the same wall: there are no public performance numbers with stated measurement conditions. Third-party cross-product benchmarks don’t exist; what you can find is either vendor-quoted partial metrics (detector inference latency, say) or editorial estimate tables that omit the hardware, bitrate, and framerate conditions — the numbers can’t be compared against each other.

So I measured MiBeeNvr’s own capacity and resource curves: three hardware tiers, recording ramps from 16 to 68 cameras, concurrent playback on top of full load, pure forwarding, an fsync-policy comparison, plus a read-only observation of a 7×24 production machine. The methodology, pass/fail criteria, and test scripts are all published with this post. The goal is not to rank products — with no comparable public methodology, ranking means nothing — but to answer two questions that actually come up during capacity planning: how many cameras a machine of a given tier can carry, and whether the bottleneck lands on CPU, memory, or storage.
